Introduction to DMAR

Ken Kelley

November 2026

Source: vignettes/DMAR.Rmd
DMAR.Rmd

What Is DMAR?

DMAR is a more general and greatly expanded reimagining of the MBESS package (Kelley, 2007a, Journal of Statistical Software; 2007b, Behavior Research Methods). MBESS itself was originally framed as Methods for the Behavioral, Educational, and Social Sciences, but the methods it implements became useful far beyond that scope; DMAR ships under a new name to make that scope expansion explicit. Its emphasis is on confidence intervals for effect sizes built from noncentral sampling distributions, sample size planning for both power and accuracy in parameter estimation (AIPE), reliability, factor analysis, and the critical values used in classical inference. DMAR is intended to serve as the computational companion to Maxwell, Delaney, and Kelley’s Designing Experiments and Analyzing Data (4th ed., 2027; henceforth MDK), for use in both instruction and substantive research.

Although the package’s origins are in psychology, the questions it answers are not field-specific. Researchers in biostatistics (clinical-trial effect size CIs and AIPE-based trial sizing), organizational behavior and management science (intervention, training, and program evaluation), information systems (user-experience A/B comparisons; technology-adoption studies), education (instructional effectiveness, longitudinal achievement gains), sociology (program evaluation, attitudinal surveys), and the methodological literature itself share the same three tasks: estimating effect sizes, constructing confidence intervals for them, and planning the sample size of future studies, for power or for the precision of an estimate.

What DMAR keeps from MBESS is the philosophy, that is, the same insistence on effect sizes with uncertainty quantified, and on planning studies for accurate estimation rather than only for sufficient power. What DMAR changes is the implementation: a uniform snake_case interface, tidy data.frame returns with consistently named columns, native ggplot2 visualization, heavier dependencies kept in Suggests and loaded only by the functions that use them, and a test suite that checks results against published values and reference implementations. The function families have also been broadened, particularly the ss_power_* family, which now covers between-subjects, within-subjects, mixed, and multilevel designs across the chapters of MDK.

Why Effect Size Confidence Intervals?

A p-value tells you whether an effect is plausibly nonzero in the direction you tested. It does not tell you how large the effect is, and it does not tell you how precisely you have estimated it. Both of those questions matter scientifically: a study can produce a “significant” but trivially small effect, or a “nonsignificant” effect whose confidence interval is so wide that it is consistent with both a small and a large true value. Reporting an effect size and a confidence interval for it addresses both shortcomings. The Publication Manual of the American Psychological Association calls for effect sizes and confidence intervals, and the reporting standards of the American Educational Research Association call for effect sizes and an indication of their uncertainty, such as a confidence interval (see the review by Kelley & Preacher, 2012).

For most standardized effect sizes, the sampling distribution is noncentral (e.g., the noncentral t underlying Cohen’s dd, the noncentral F underlying R2R^2, the noncentral χ2\chi^2 underlying RMSEA), which means the exact interval, under the model’s assumptions, is asymmetric about the point estimate. The symmetric “estimate ±\pm standard error” approximation ignores that skew. DMAR computes the intervals for these effect sizes from the noncentral distributions directly, through the routines that ci_nc_t(), ci_nc_F(), and ci_nc_chisq() expose.

Two Philosophies of Sample Size Planning

Researchers who plan studies in DMAR can do so from either of two complementary perspectives:

  • Power. Functions in the ss_power_* family answer the question “How many subjects do I need so that, if the effect in the population is what I expect, I have at least probability π\pi of rejecting the null?” This is the familiar Cohen-style framing.
  • Accuracy in parameter estimation (AIPE). Functions in the ss_aipe_* family answer a different question: “How many subjects do I need so that the confidence interval around my effect size estimate is no wider than ww?” AIPE is appropriate when estimation is the primary goal, for example, when an effect is already known to be nonzero and the next study should pin down its magnitude rather than re-establish significance.

Accuracy has a specific meaning in this framework, and the term is sometimes used loosely. Accuracy considers precision and bias together: an accurate estimator is one whose sampling distribution is concentrated and centered on the target parameter. Precision alone, in contrast, can always be improved by trading bias for precision. A trivial estimator that returns the same constant value for every sample has zero variance and is therefore arbitrarily “precise,” but it is biased unless the constant happens to equal the population parameter. The AIPE framing asks for sample sizes that buy narrow confidence intervals (a precision target) without trading bias to get there. The confidence interval width target ww in ss_aipe_* is shorthand for that joint accuracy goal: a CI that is informative because it is both narrow and centered on the parameter (Kelley & Rausch, 2006; Kelley & Maxwell, 2003; Maxwell, Kelley, & Rausch, 2008).

The two perspectives often imply different sample sizes for the same study, and which is larger depends on the width chosen and on the size of the effect. DMAR provides both side by side so that the choice can be made deliberately, in light of the scientific question.

When Do You Reach for DMAR?

The package is organized around six families of tasks. Pick the one that matches the question you are trying to answer.

1. I Just Ran an ANOVA, t-Test, or Regression. What’s the Effect Size and a CI for It?

Use the ci_* family.

# Confidence interval for omega squared (proportion of variance accounted
# for) from a one-way ANOVA with F = 11.221 on (4, 50) df, total N = 55.
# F determines the partial value, which in a one-way design is the total.
ci_omega_squared(F_value = 11.221, df_effect = 4, df_error = 50, N = 55,
                 estimand = "partial")
effect omega_squared_partial omega_squared_partial_ci_lower omega_squared_partial_ci_upper F_value df_effect df_error N
overall 0.426 0.226 0.587 11.221 4 50 55

Confidence level: 95%


# More naturally, from a fitted model:
fit <- aov(log_drinks ~ treatment, data = drinks_trial)
ci_omega_squared(fit)
effect omega_squared_total omega_squared_total_ci_lower omega_squared_total_ci_upper omega_squared_partial omega_squared_partial_ci_lower omega_squared_partial_ci_upper F_value df_effect df_error N
treatment 0.069 0.002 0.207 0.069 0.002 0.207 4.261 2 85 88

Confidence level: 95%

The fitted model is a one-way ANOVA of the drinks_trial data, from the randomized clinical trial of the Community Reinforcement Approach (CRA) with 88 homeless alcohol-dependent individuals reported by Smith, Meyers, and Delaney (1998) and reproduced in MDK (Chapter 3). Participants were randomized to CRA, to CRA augmented with disulfiram, or to standard care. The outcome, log_drinks, is the common log of one plus the average number of standard drinks per week at the nine-month follow-up; the raw averages are markedly right-skewed, and the primary published analyses were run on this scale. The trial enrolled two consecutive cohorts and ran the disulfiram arm in the first only. To keep the demonstration a one-way design, the analysis here and in section 3 pools the two cohorts. That is a simplification: the contrasts that ?drinks_trial suggests compare CRA with CRA plus disulfiram within Cohort 1, the only cohort in which all three arms ran, and pool the cohorts only for CRA against standard care.

The output is a tidy data.frame: an effect label, the point estimate (omega_squared), the lower and upper limits of the CI, and the inputs that produced it (F_value, df_effect, df_error, and N). That format can be passed directly to a table or to a forest plot (plot_ci() takes it as input).

CI variants exist for many other effect sizes: ci_smd() for the standardized mean difference (Cohen’s dd); ci_smd_c() for the standardized mean difference using the control-group SD as the divisor; ci_pvaf() for the proportion of variance in the outcome accounted for by the levels of a factor; ci_snr() and ci_srsnr() for signal-to-noise ratios; ci_r() and ci_R() for the correlation and the multiple correlation; ci_R2() for the squared multiple correlation; ci_rc() and ci_src() for unstandardized and standardized regression coefficients; ci_rmsea() for the RMSEA model-fit index; and others.

2. I’m Planning a Study. How Many Subjects Do I Need?

Use ss_power_* for sufficient power, or ss_aipe_* for sufficient precision. The same effect can be approached from either angle.

# Power-based: per-group n needed for 90% power to detect a contrast among
# 4 groups with population means (90, 92, 88, 81) and within-group
# variance 144. The contrast compares the average of the first three
# groups against the fourth.
ss_power_contrast(
  c_weights           = c(1/3, 1/3, 1/3, -1),
  true_means          = c(90, 92, 88, 81),
  true_var_error = 144,
  desired_power       = 0.90
)
term value
necessary_n_per_group 26
total_N 104
actual_power 0.907
noncentral_t_parm 3.312
true_f 0.325 
# AIPE-based: n needed so a 95% CI around a population standardized mean
# difference of 0.50 is no wider than 0.30 units (a tight interval).
ss_aipe_smd(true_smd = 0.50, conf_level = 0.95, width = 0.30)
term value
necessary_n_per_group 353
true_smd 0.500
width 0.300

Confidence level: 95%

The ss_power_* family spans most of the standard designs covered in MDK: one-way ANOVA (ss_power_one_way_anova), factorial ANOVA (ss_power_factorial_anova), repeated measures ANOVA with sphericity adjustment (ss_power_rm_anova), split-plot mixed ANOVA (ss_power_split_plot_anova), Pearson correlation (ss_power_r), two-independent-groups standardized mean difference (ss_power_smd), contrasts standardized and unstandardized (ss_power_c, ss_power_sc, ss_power_c_ancova, ss_power_contrast), regression coefficients (ss_power_reg_coef), and two-level random-intercept models for cluster-randomized trials (ss_power_mixed_effects). For SEM-style designs, use ss_power_sem(). AIPE counterparts exist for the correspondingly named effects.

3. I Want to Test a Specific Contrast or Set of Pairwise Comparisons.

Use contrast_test() for arbitrary contrasts in a one-way ANOVA, with optional multiple-comparison adjustment.

fit <- aov(log_drinks ~ treatment, data = drinks_trial)
# All pairwise comparisons, Tukey-protected family-wise error rate:
contrast_test(fit, contrasts = "pairwise", adjust = "tukey")
contrast estimate se t_value df p_value p_adjusted ci_lower ci_upper
CRA - Standard -0.454 0.198 -2.294 85 0.0242 0.0620 -0.927 0.018
CRA + Disulfiram - Standard -0.594 0.232 -2.567 85 0.0120 0.0319 -1.147 -0.042
CRA + Disulfiram - CRA -0.140 0.238 -0.589 85 0.5575 0.8264 -0.707 0.427

Confidence level: 95%, simultaneous interval (Tukey)

For the bare critical value of a particular procedure, see the cv_* family: cv_t(), cv_tukey_hsd(), cv_scheffe(), cv_smm() (the studentized maximum modulus), cv_dunnett(), and cv_z(). These return the threshold value alone, suitable for inclusion in user code or hand-checking textbook examples.

4. I Have Within-Subjects (Repeated Measures) Data.

Start with anova_within(), which combines the univariate within-subjects F test with a sphericity diagnostic (Mauchly’s W) and the three standard ε\varepsilon-corrected p-values (Greenhouse-Geisser, Huynh-Feldt, lower-bound). The motivation is that an uncorrected within-subjects F test can be substantially anticonservative when the sphericity assumption fails, and anova_within() puts the diagnostic and the correction in one place.

The pygmalion data are the teacher-expectancy data from Rosenthal and Jacobson’s (1968) Pygmalion in the Classroom: intelligence test scores for 310 elementary school children in grades 1 through 6, of whom 64 were randomly designated to their teachers as likely “intellectual bloomers” while the remaining 246 served as controls. Each child’s total IQ was measured three times: at the pretest (iq_pre), at an intermediate follow-up assessment (iq_4), and at the end-of-study follow-up assessment (iq_8). The three occasions are the levels of a within-subjects factor. anova_within() takes the scores in long form, one row per child per occasion, with a column that identifies the child:

n_children <- nrow(pygmalion)
occasions  <- c("pretest", "intermediate", "end_of_study")
iq_long <- data.frame(
  id       = factor(rep(seq_len(n_children), times = 3)),
  occasion = factor(rep(occasions, each = n_children), levels = occasions),
  iq       = c(pygmalion$iq_pre, pygmalion$iq_4, pygmalion$iq_8)
)
res <- anova_within(iq_long, id = "id", time = "occasion", outcome = "iq")
res
adjustment F_value df_1 df_2 p_value epsilon
none 83.113 2 618 < 0.0001 NA
Greenhouse-Geisser 83.113 1.928 595.813 < 0.0001 0.964
Huynh-Feldt 83.113 1.940 599.482 < 0.0001 0.970
lower_bound 83.113 1 309 < 0.0001 0.500 
attr(res, "mauchly")
W statistic df p_value n_subjects n_levels method
0.963 11.689 2 0.0029 310 3 Mauchly’s test of sphericity

With 310 children, Mauchly’s test is sensitive to small departures from sphericity (W = 0.963, p = 0.0029), and the departure here is small: the Greenhouse-Geisser and Huynh-Feldt estimates of ε\varepsilon are 0.964 and 0.970, near their upper bound of 1, so the corrected tests differ little from the uncorrected one.

anova_within() keeps the partial η2\eta^2 for occasion, a point estimate, in its eta_squared_partial attribute. Its confidence interval comes from ci_eta_squared(estimand = "partial"), which takes the same analysis fitted by aov() with an Error() term for the children and returns one row per effect, naming the error stratum that the row’s F was tested against:

fit_rm <- aov(iq ~ occasion + Error(id / occasion), data = iq_long)
ci_occasion <- ci_eta_squared(fit_rm, estimand = "partial")
ci_occasion
effect eta_squared_partial eta_squared_partial_ci_lower eta_squared_partial_ci_upper stratum F_value df_effect df_error N
occasion 0.212 0.157 0.265 id:occasion 83.113 2 618 930

Confidence level: 95%

The interval is built from the uncorrected F on 2 and 618 degrees of freedom (the none row of the anova_within() table), so like the uncorrected test it takes sphericity as given; with ε\varepsilon this near 1, the corrected degrees of freedom are close to these. The partial η2\eta^2 is the proportion of the within-child variance in IQ that the occasions account for, since its denominator leaves out the variation due to stable differences among the children.

Mean IQ rose from 98.5 at the pretest to 101.7 at the intermediate follow-up and 107.9 at the end of the study, Huynh-Feldt corrected F(1.94, 599.48) = 83.11, p < 0.0001, partial η2\eta^2 = 0.212, 95% CI [0.157, 0.265].

The analysis pools the bloomers and the controls, so it asks whether the children’s mean IQ changed across the three occasions, not whether the expectancy manipulation changed it. That question compares the two conditions, and the analysis of covariance these data are best known for takes it up in vignette("pygmalion").

For the underlying components separately, see mauchly_test() and epsilon_corrections(). For visualizing individual subject trajectories, see plot_trajectories() and plot_trajectories_fitted().

5. I Want Descriptive Statistics, a Correlation Table, or Distribution-Shape Diagnostics.

descriptives() returns a tidy summary suitable for screening. Here it screens six tests from holzinger_swineford, the scores of 301 seventh and eighth grade pupils at two Chicago elementary schools on 26 ability tests (Holzinger & Swineford, 1939): three spatial tests and three verbal ones, the six that the measurement model of the next section takes up. Short names for the tests keep the correlation table below narrow.

ability_tests <- setNames(
  holzinger_swineford[, c("t1_visual_perception", "t2_cubes", "t4_lozenges",
                          "t6_paragraph_comprehension", "t7_sentence",
                          "t9_word_meaning")],
  c("visual", "cubes", "lozenges", "paragraph", "sentence", "word_meaning")
)
descriptives(ability_tests)$descriptives

The three verbal tests correlate more strongly with one another than any of them does with a spatial test. The spatial tests hang together less tightly, so the clustering that the two-factor model of the next section describes is clearest on the verbal side.

For interrater agreement, use cohen_kappa() (two raters), fleiss_kappa() (multiple raters), or icc() (intraclass correlation, all six classical forms). For distribution-shape statistics in isolation, use skewness() and kurtosis().

6. I Am Developing a Measurement Model.

Use a common-factor model for the shared variation among items. fa_exploratory() returns rotated loadings, factor correlations, and communalities with confidence intervals, and prints them as a solution: the loadings matrix with intervals, each item’s complexity, the variance each factor accounts for, the factor correlations, each factor’s determinacy and coefficient H with intervals, and the fit, whose RMSEA interval is at 90 percent, the conventional level for that index (rmsea_conf_level), where the other intervals are at 95 percent. With continuous incomplete observations it fits the raw data by FIML, rather than treating an estimated correlation matrix as a complete-data sample covariance.

measurement_items <- c("t1_visual_perception", "t2_cubes", "t4_lozenges",
  "t6_paragraph_comprehension", "t7_sentence", "t9_word_meaning")
exploratory <- fa_exploratory(holzinger_swineford, nfactors = 2,
                              items = measurement_items, seed = 113)
exploratory

Intervals condition on the selected factor count and rotation.

These intervals condition on the chosen factor count and rotation. The count itself is a judgment, and factor_count() sets what bears on it side by side: for one factor, two, and so on, the fit of that model and the test of the previous count against it, its information criteria, the reduced eigenvalue at that rank against its parallel analysis reference, and Velicer’s minimum average partial. The parallel analysis reference percentile is a null threshold, not a sampling confidence interval for an observed eigenvalue or for the count, and the table applies no cutoff.

factor_count(holzinger_swineford, items = measurement_items, B = 200,
             seed = 113)

Factor counts 1 to 2 for 6 items, N = 301

Estimator: ML; missing data: FIML; unrotated solutions (the fit of a count does not depend on the rotation)

factors solution chi_square df p_value rmsea cfi tli srmr bic delta weight p_delta eigenvalue reference map

2 proper 2.109 4 0.7157 0.000 [0.000, 0.064] 1.000 1.011 0.008 10981.9 0.0 1.000 < 0.0001 0.568 0.170 0.102

(each count’s model: chi square test, RMSEA with 90% interval, CFI, TLI, SRMR, BIC with delta (its gap from the lowest) and weight (its relative weight among the proper solutions); p_delta: the test of the previous count against this one; eigenvalue: of the reduced correlation matrix, with its parallel analysis 95th percentile; map: Velicer’s average squared partial correlation after this many components)

Information criteria over the proper solutions: lowest AIC at 2 factors, lowest BIC at 2 factors, lowest SABIC at 2 factors.

BIC comparison over the proper solutions (compare_sem()): lowest at 2 factors, weight 1.000; the nearest other count, 1 factor, is 72.6 higher (weight 0.000, log Bayes factor 36.3 for 2 factors over it).

Parallel analysis (normal reference, B = 200, 95th percentile, reference N = 301): the reduced eigenvalues exceed their reference through rank 2.

Velicer’s MAP: the average squared partial correlation is smallest after 2 components (0.102; before any component is removed it is 0.164).

Confidence level: 90%

No cutoff is applied and no count is chosen: the count is a judgment that combines the fit of each model, the difference tests, the information criteria, the eigenvalues against their reference, and the MAP with theory and the interpretability of the rotated solutions, which fa_exploratory() gives at a chosen count. Each model’s interval and p-values condition on its own count, and the criterion weights are conditional on the set of proper counts compared.

Once a measurement structure is supported, a latent SEM estimates relations among constructs without treating factor scores as error-free. Local structural-after-measurement estimation is another option. sem_sam() fits measurement blocks first and propagates their uncertainty through two-step SEs for the structural parameters (Rosseel & Loh, 2024). Its current scope is complete continuous data; incomplete-data uncertainty and arbitrary cross-stage derived effects are refused rather than silently approximated.

model <- "visual =~ t1_visual_perception + t2_cubes + t4_lozenges
          verbal =~ t6_paragraph_comprehension + t7_sentence + t9_word_meaning
          verbal ~ visual"
sem_sam(model, holzinger_swineford, estimator = "MLR")

Confidence level: 95%

Local SAM: MLR; SE: twostep.robust; complete continuous data; gamma_unbiased = TRUE. Intervals concern individual original-unit parameters. Cross-stage covariance cells are incomplete; do not use the attached fit for arbitrary derived or standardized structural intervals.

ML and MLR use the same likelihood objective here. Their SEs differ because normal-theory and sandwich inference make different covariance assumptions, not because one point estimate was computed iteratively. A bootstrap is a separate uncertainty procedure and should be named explicitly when used.

What DMAR Is Not

DMAR deliberately overlaps with, but does not duplicate, several specialized packages.

  • For full-featured factor analysis and SEM, use lavaan.
  • For coefficient α\alpha / ω\omega with extensive options, use psych::omega().
  • For mixed-effects models, use lme4 or nlme.
  • For robust ANOVA, use WRS2.

DMAR layers tidy effect size CIs, sample size planning, and publication-ready output over those tools, rather than replacing them.

A Note on Argument Naming

The package uses snake_case throughout. Capital letters in identifiers are reserved for two uses. The first is statistically meaningful symbols, for example R2 for the squared multiple correlation, N for total sample size, S for a covariance matrix, F_value for an F statistic, B and G for the numbers of bootstrap and Monte Carlo replications, and M for item means. The second is the labels of variables, factors, and groups, for example X, Y, and Z (as in true_mean_Y and true_cor_YX), A and B for the factors of a two-factor design (as in factor_A), and C for a control group (as in mean_C). A population value given to a planner carries the prefix true_ and an English name for the quantity, and the planning value a sensitivity function chooses its design under carries the prefix supposed_, so examples read consistently regardless of discipline:

ci_R2(R2 = 0.25, N = 100, p = 5, random_predictors = TRUE)
ss_power_reg_coef(true_R2_Y_X = 0.78, true_R2_Y_X_without_j = 0.74,
                  p = 5, desired_power = 0.85)
ss_aipe_cv_sensitivity(true_cv = 0.25, supposed_cv = 0.25,
                       width = 0.10, conf_level = 0.95, G = 200)

DMAR does not accept the MBESS dot.case style (conf.level, Random.Predictors, Specified.N). Scripts written against MBESS will need to convert dots to underscores in argument names and lowercase any prefix words that are not themselves statistical notation. Many function names carry over with underscores in place of dots (ci.smd() is ci_smd(), ss.aipe.reg.coef() is ss_aipe_reg_coef()), and results are returned as data frames rather than lists (see vignette("mbess_to_dmar")).

If you have scripts written against MBESS and you see errors of the form

Error in foo(...) : unused argument (Group.1 = ...)

the first step is to replace dots with underscores in the argument name (Group_1, n_1, Mean_1, Specified_N, etc.) and then lowercase the capitalized prefix words that are not statistical notation (group_1, mean_1, specified_N, …). Some arguments are also named for the role the value plays: the population standardized mean difference that MBESS’s ss.aipe.smd() takes as delta is true_smd in ss_aipe_smd().

The single convention exists for one reason: a mix of dot.case and snake_case arguments is confusing in side-by-side examples, especially in teaching.
